findings.description: README says "Thirteen routes under `/edge` each make one thing go wrong on purpose," but `app/edge/` only contains eleven route directories (action, divergent, double-count, invalidate, leakage, middleware, mixed-payload, suspense, unregistered, version-skew, wrong-subject), and the index page's own EDGES list (app/page.tsx) also enumerates exactly eleven. A reader trusting the count would expect two more scenarios than exist.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "Thirteen" to "Eleven" (or add the missing routes if two were intended but never built).

findings.description: The doc comment on `canWriteArticle` says "Draft editing, used by the server action route," but no server action or route in the example ever references `canWriteArticle` (`src/server/actions.ts` only uses `canPublishArticle`). The policy is only reachable via the `catalogue` map for the devtools Policy explorer — it is never actually enforced anywhere, contrary to what the comment claims.
findings.suggestedFix: Either wire `canWriteArticle` into a real write-guarding route/action, or correct the comment to say it exists for the catalogue/Policy explorer only.

findings.description: The comment claims "`embargoLifted` is `false` here" for `policyResource(article, 0)`, but `policyResource` computes `embargoLifted: nowMillis >= article.embargoUntil`. Three of the four demo articles have `embargoUntil: 0`, so `0 >= 0` evaluates to `true`, not `false` — only "the-tender" (far-future embargo) actually gets `false`. The comment misdescribes the runtime value for most of the fixture data, even though the surrounding point (nothing has to match a server-side decision key) is still true.
findings.suggestedFix: Correct the comment to state that `embargoLifted` is computed against `nowMillis=0` and varies per article (true for unembargoed articles, false for "the-tender"), rather than asserting it is uniformly false.

findings.description: Grammar typo in fixture body text: "a evaluation committee of two" should be "an evaluation committee of two."

`RESTRICTED_FIELDS` is exported and its comment says it is "named once," implying `PUBLIC_FIELDS` or a policy derives from it, but nothing in the example ever imports or references `RESTRICTED_FIELDS` — `PUBLIC_FIELDS` is defined independently instead. Because it's a module-level export rather than a local, `noUnusedLocals`/`noUnusedParameters` do not catch it, so it silently rots.
findings.suggestedFix: Either derive `PUBLIC_FIELDS` from `RESTRICTED_FIELDS` (or vice versa) so the two stay in sync, or remove the unused export.

findings.description: `allPermissions` is exported but never imported or referenced anywhere else in the example (no catalogue, page, or test uses it). Module-level exports aren't flagged by `noUnusedLocals`, so this has no build-time signal.
findings.suggestedFix: Either wire `allPermissions` into the dock's `catalogue` (if a permissions listing was intended) or remove it.

findings.description: `redactArticle` is defined and granted to the Editor and ChiefEditor roles (src/domain/roles.ts:16,35), but no policy in the example ever checks `hasPermission(redactArticle)`. It shows up on the Roles screen's provenance column as a grant with nothing behind it to demonstrate, unlike every other permission in `allPermissions` which has a corresponding policy.
findings.suggestedFix: Either add a small policy/route exercising `redactArticle` (matching the file's stated goal of covering every mechanism) or drop it from the roles until one exists.

findings.description: The `paths: { "~/*": ["./src/*"] }` alias is declared but no file in the example imports via `~/...` — every import uses relative paths with explicit `.ts`/`.tsx` extensions, per this repo's own convention. Dead configuration that could confuse a reader into thinking the alias is the intended import style.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the unused `paths` entry, or start using it consistently and note the exception to the relative-import convention.

findings.description: `field()` reads one named property off an unknown JSON body via `Object.entries(body).find(([name]) => name === key)?.[1]`, an O(n) scan of every property instead of a direct lookup. Harmless at today's payload sizes (a handful of fields) but an odd, non-obvious way to read one field — a reader might assume there's a reason for the scan (e.g. duplicate keys) when there isn't.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a small type guard (`(body: unknown): body is Record<string, unknown> => typeof body === "object" && body !== null`) and then index directly, e.g. `isRecord(body) ? body[key] : undefined`, which avoids `as` without the O(n) scan.

findings.description: `decideAs`'s helper pipes the real `decide(...)` evaluation call through `Effect.orDie`. AGENTS.md §4 states "Never `Effect.orDie` in evaluation or enforcement paths — an authorization decision must never become a defect," and `decide` is literally the evaluation function, unlike the `Layer.orDie` uses in `src/server/ports.ts`/`src/client/ports.ts` which are explicitly justified as construction-time-only. This one is test-fixture code where a defect on setup failure is arguably fine, but it isn't called out as an exception the way the other two `orDie` usages in this example are.
findings.suggestedFix: Either replace `Effect.orDie` with a targeted `Effect.catchTag`/`Effect.die` with an explanatory comment (mirroring ports.ts's justification), or leave as-is with a one-line comment noting it's test-fixture-only and why that's an acceptable exception.
